prompt: OWASP Top 10:2025: match each description to its category.

pairs.item: A user can read or change a resource without the required permission
pairs.why: Using a resource without permission is broken access control.

pairs.item: Settings expose data or features more widely than intended
pairs.why: Exposure caused by settings is misconfiguration.

pairs.item: Dependencies, suppliers, build systems or updates introduce risk
pairs.why: Risk from suppliers, dependencies and builds is supply chain.

pairs.item: Sensitive data lacks suitable protection in transit or storage
pairs.why: Weak protection of data in transit or storage is cryptographic.

pairs.item: Untrusted input changes the meaning of a query, command or page
pairs.why: Input changing a query, command or page is injection.

explanation: Each category gives the team a useful question to ask about its own application.

prompt: OWASP Top 10:2025: match each description to its category.

pairs.item: A necessary security rule is missing from the workflow or architecture
pairs.why: A missing rule in the workflow is insecure design.

pairs.item: Login or session handling does not reliably establish and maintain identity
pairs.why: Unreliable login or sessions are authentication failures.

pairs.item: Software or data is accepted without checking it is authentic and unchanged
pairs.why: Using unverified software or data is an integrity failure.

pairs.item: Relevant events are not recorded, noticed or acted on
pairs.why: Events nobody notices or acts on are logging and alerting failures.

pairs.item: Errors, outages or unusual states cause unsafe behaviour
pairs.why: Unsafe behaviour on errors is mishandling exceptional conditions.

explanation: The categories are an awareness and planning resource; they do not replace reviewing your own application's features, data and users.

prompt: Match each scenario to the OWASP category it illustrates.

pairs.item: Changing a sequential document number in a URL shows other customers' documents, with no login
pairs.why: No permission check on each document is broken access control.

pairs.item: Customer data in cloud storage is reachable from the internet because of its settings
pairs.why: Exposure through storage settings is misconfiguration.

pairs.item: Malicious code is inserted into a trusted vendor's software update
pairs.why: A compromised vendor update is a supply chain failure.

pairs.item: Stolen password hashes were made with a fast, unsalted hash and many are cracked
pairs.why: Fast, unsalted password hashes are a cryptographic failure.

pairs.item: Crafted input changes a database query and the attacker then installs a web shell
pairs.why: Crafted input changing a query is injection.

explanation: Start with what went wrong: a missing permission check, unsafe settings, a compromised supplier, weak protection of secrets, or input changing a query.

prompt: Match each scenario to the OWASP category it illustrates.

pairs.item: The purchase workflow has no rule against bots and bulk accounts, so buyers get around a per-customer limit
pairs.why: The workflow lacks a rule against automated bulk buying, so it's a design gap.

pairs.item: Attackers log in using passwords reused from other breached sites
pairs.why: Reused stolen passwords working is an authentication failure.

pairs.item: A downloaded build script was modified; its hash no longer matches the published value
pairs.why: Running a modified script without verifying it is an integrity failure.

pairs.item: Traffic inspection quietly stops working and nobody is alerted, so data theft goes unnoticed for weeks
pairs.why: A signal nobody is alerted to is a logging and alerting failure.

pairs.item: A service the login depends on goes down, and the error-handling code lets users in without the second factor
pairs.why: Letting users in when MFA errors is mishandling an exceptional condition.

explanation: Start with what went wrong: a missing rule in the workflow, weak login protection, an unverified artifact, a signal nobody acted on, or unsafe behaviour when something failed.

prompt: Match each scenario to its OWASP category.

pairs.item: An API updates whichever account ID is in the request body without checking ownership
pairs.why: No ownership check is broken access control.

pairs.item: A production server keeps a sample admin console with its default password
pairs.why: A leftover default login is misconfiguration.

pairs.item: A web app ships an unsupported library with a known exploitable flaw
pairs.why: A known-vulnerable dependency is a supply chain failure.

pairs.item: The login page sends passwords over plain, unencrypted HTTP
pairs.why: Passwords sent unencrypted are a cryptographic failure.

pairs.item: A user's comment is inserted into a page without context-aware output encoding
pairs.why: Unencoded user input in a page is injection.

explanation: No ownership check is access control. A leftover default login is misconfiguration. A known-vulnerable dependency is supply chain. Plain HTTP for passwords is a cryptographic failure. Unencoded user input in a page is injection.

prompt: Match each scenario to its OWASP category.

pairs.item: By design, the account-recovery workflow accepts the answer to a security question that other people can find out
pairs.why: A weak recovery rule built into the workflow is insecure design.

pairs.item: A session token still works after the user logs out
pairs.why: A token that survives logout is an authentication failure.

pairs.item: A server deserialises a user-controlled object and trusts an unsigned role field inside it
pairs.why: Trusting an unsigned field is an integrity failure.

pairs.item: An account exports thousands of records overnight; events are logged but nobody is alerted
pairs.why: Logged but unalerted activity is a logging and alerting failure.

pairs.item: A payment debits one account, fails before crediting the other, and is not rolled back
pairs.why: A half-finished payment with no rollback is mishandling an exceptional condition.

explanation: A weak recovery rule built into the workflow is insecure design. A token that survives logout is an authentication failure. Trusting an unsigned field is an integrity failure. Logged but unalerted activity is a logging and alerting failure. A half-finished payment with no rollback is mishandling an exceptional condition.

prompt: What distinguishes Software Supply Chain Failures from Software or Data Integrity Failures?

options.text: Supply chain covers suppliers, dependencies and builds; integrity covers checking one artifact before use
Supply chain covers only outdated packages; integrity covers all other third-party code
options.why: Supply chain risk covers suppliers, dependencies and builds, not just outdated packages.

options.text: Supply chain is about encrypting downloads; integrity is about logging who changed them
options.why: Neither category is about encryption or logging; they concern trusted sources and verified artifacts.

options.text: They are the same category, renamed in the 2025 edition of the OWASP list
options.why: They are separate categories that often overlap on the same event.

explanation: Supply chain risk is broader than old packages: suppliers, dependencies, build systems and update routes. Integrity is about verifying a specific artifact or data object before use.

prompt: An attacker modifies a supplier's update and customers install it. Which OWASP categories can this involve?

options.text: Software Supply Chain Failures and Software or Data Integrity Failures
Broken Access Control and Authentication Failures
options.why: Nobody's access was bypassed and no login failed; the trusted update itself was modified.

options.text: Injection only
options.why: No untrusted input changed a query or command; the software artifact was altered.

options.text: Security Logging and Alerting Failures and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
options.why: Logging and error handling may matter later, but the core failures are the supply chain and the unverified update.

explanation: Categories overlap. The supply chain and the integrity of the downloaded artifact are different questions about the same event.

prompt: An application stores user passwords as plain SHA-1 hashes with no salt. What should it do instead?

options.text: Hash them with a password hash such as Argon2id, with a random salt each
Encrypt them with AES so they can be recovered if users forget
options.why: Passwords should never be recoverable; encryption means anyone with the key can read them all.

options.text: Switch to SHA-256, which is a newer and stronger hash than SHA-1
options.why: SHA-256 is still a fast hash, so guessing stays cheap; passwords need a slow, salted password hash.

options.text: Base64-encode them so they are no longer stored as readable text
options.why: Base64 is reversible encoding, not protection.

explanation: Hashing and encryption have different purposes. Passwords need a costly, salted password hash; encryption is for data that must be recovered later.

prompt: If attackers log in using passwords reused from other breaches, the site's own password database must have been breached.
explanation: Credential stuffing uses credentials stolen elsewhere. Defend with MFA, throttling repeated attempts, and session expiry or invalidation.

prompt: How can a team check that a downloaded build tool has not been tampered with before running it?

options.text: Compare its hash or signature with a trusted published value
Check that the file extension matches what the vendor's website says
options.why: An extension is just a name; a tampered file can keep the expected extension.

options.text: Run it once in a production environment and watch closely for errors
options.why: Running untrusted code in production is exactly the risk you're trying to avoid.

options.text: Check that the download size matches what other users have reported
options.why: A malicious version can easily have a similar size; only a trusted hash or signature verifies content.

explanation: Software or Data Integrity Failures asks whether a particular artifact is authentic and unchanged before use.

prompt: A team says, "We log everything, so Security Logging and Alerting is covered." Why is that not enough?

options.text: Someone also has to notice the events, escalate them and act on them
Logs only count if they are stored in a cloud service
options.why: Where logs are stored doesn't matter if nobody is alerted and acts on them.

options.text: Only failed logins need logging, so the rest is wasted
options.why: Many events beyond failed logins matter, such as permission changes and bulk exports.

options.text: Logging everything is itself a vulnerability to be fixed
options.why: Logging isn't the vulnerability; the gap is that nobody notices or responds.

explanation: Test the whole event-to-alert path, including whether staff can see and respond to the signal.

prompt: Which controls address injection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bind SQL values as parameters
Encode browser output for its context
Use a password-specific hash
options.why: Password hashing protects stored passwords; it doesn't stop input changing a query or page.

options.text: Enable multi-factor authentication
options.why: MFA protects login; injection happens in how input is handled after login.

options.text: Keep tested backups
options.why: Backups help recovery afterwards; they don't stop input changing a query or page.

explanation: Parameters protect the database query and output encoding protects the page. They address different interpreters, so one does not replace the other: parameterised SQL does nothing to stop XSS.

prompt: The design already includes a per-customer purchase limit, but the code for one endpoint forgets to apply it. Is this a missing design rule or an implementation defect?

options.text: An implementation defect: the rule exists, but the code doesn’t apply it
Insecure design: the rule must be missing from the design
options.why: The rule is in the design, so this isn't insecure design; the code failed to apply it.

options.text: Security misconfiguration: a server setting is switched off
options.why: No server setting is involved; the endpoint's code skips a designed rule.

options.text: A logging failure: nobody was alerted when the limit was skipped
options.why: Missing alerts might delay detection, but the cause is the code not applying the rule.

explanation: Insecure Design means a necessary security rule is missing from the workflow or architecture. Here the rule exists in the design; the implementation failed to apply it.

prompt: Which test best checks an application for broken access control?

options.text: Try reading and changing records with two different accounts
Run a password-cracking tool against the stored password hashes
options.why: Password cracking tests password storage, not whether users can reach others' records.

options.text: Check that error pages hide stack traces and version numbers
options.why: Hiding stack traces is about error disclosure, not access control.

options.text: Check every dependency version against a vulnerability feed
options.why: Dependency checks find vulnerable components, not missing permission checks.

explanation: Does the server check the user, resource and action on each request?

prompt: A user can be correctly authenticated and still not be authorised to view another user's profile.
explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorisation controls which resources that identity can use. Authentication Failures and Broken Access Control need separate checks.

prompt: Which of these are examples of security misconfiguration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unnecessary services
Default accounts
Verbose error messages
Cloud permissions wider than intended
Unsalted password hashes
options.why: Unsalted password hashes are a cryptographic failure in how passwords are stored, not a configuration setting.

explanation: Unsalted password hashes are a cryptographic failure, not a misconfiguration.

prompt: Production error pages show full stack traces and framework versions. Which OWASP category fits best?

options.text: Security Misconfiguration
Software Supply Chain Failures
options.why: Supply chain concerns third-party components and updates, not what error pages reveal.

options.text: Cryptographic Failures
options.why: Nothing here involves weak encryption; the server is showing too much detail.

options.text: Insecure Design
options.why: Insecure design is a missing rule in the workflow; this is a deployment setting left on.

explanation: Misconfiguration includes unnecessary services, default accounts and verbose error messages.

prompt: When the authorisation service times out, the application's error-handling code lets the request through so users are not interrupted. Which OWASP category is this?

options.text: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
Security Logging and Alerting Failures
options.why: Logging may also be weak, but the failure here is letting requests through when an error happens.

options.text: Software Supply Chain Failures
options.why: No third-party component or update is involved; the problem is the error-handling decision.

options.text: Injection
options.why: No untrusted input changes a query or command; the app fails open on a timeout.

explanation: This is failing open on an error. Decide deliberately what happens when a dependency fails: deny unsafe access, record the event and alert.

prompt: Following the OWASP Top 10 removes the need to review your own application's features, data and users.
explanation: It is an awareness and planning resource. The categories prompt useful questions; they do not replace a review of the actual application.
